prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Meninas, Pablo, Picasso

outputs.L1:
“I would try to do it in my way, forgetting Velázquez. . . . So, little by little, I would paint my Meninas . . . they would be ‘my’ Meninas.”  
—Pablo Picasso

My meninas are as changeable as the moon.  
Black and white, and in color.  
Happy, sad—and how many words there are  
for red enough, and for the pallor of skin.  
Their moments of verisimilitude do not outweigh  
their flashes of pathos. Whole days go by  
when they cannot appreciate the humor  
of which the dog is one manner, the dwarf another.  
My meninas are not puppets, but puppet theaters.  
That it is the puppet master who draws the curtain  
in the stairwell is pure whimsy on my part.  
A minuet of despair, an andante of foolhardiness.  
How many times have I tried to explain these differences:  
the sting of joy, a lilt of crimson,  
the dark and the light of the moon not the moon,  
the soul, but a sphere predisposed to rotation?  
The man in the doorway. The dog who lies sleeping.  
These are my meninas. The sun in the mirror.  
The sun and the moon and the man behind the easel,  
mostly invisible, like the pictures on the wall.  
The moon is not more changeable, however,  
than they, my meninas, who never stop changing  
and waiting on the children of the sun  
and of the moon, for they will always be  
my meninas, their eyes of every minim on the palette,  
blue and tragical, white on white against  
a black ground, until the moon sings every shape  
and shade of gray from hope to ample. And again.
outputs.L2:
Picasso said that he would approach the work in his own fashion, setting Velázquez aside, and that, gradually, he would create his own version of the Meninas.

My Meninas shift constantly, as the moon seems to do. They appear in black and white, and also in color. They can seem joyful or sorrowful, and there are countless ways to name the depth of red or the paleness of flesh. Their brief suggestions of realism are less important than the sudden sorrow they reveal. Entire days pass when they fail to notice the comedy around them: the dog embodies one kind of humor, the dwarf another.

My Meninas are not mere dolls; they are entire stages for dolls. If I imagine the puppeteer opening the curtain in the stairway, that invention is simply my own fancy. There is a dance of hopelessness here, a measured movement of reckless courage. Again and again I have tried to describe these distinctions: the sharpness inside happiness, the musical rise of red, the moon’s darkness and brightness that are not truly the moon, the soul imagined as a turning globe.

The man standing in the doorway. The dog asleep on the floor. These are my Meninas. The sun reflected in the mirror. The sun, the moon, and the nearly hidden figure behind the easel, scarcely seen, like the paintings hanging on the wall. Yet the moon is no more mutable than they are: my Meninas, endlessly transforming, forever attending the children of the sun and the moon. They will always remain mine, with eyes made from every smallest tone on the painter’s palette: blue and mournful, white layered on white against black, until the moon gives voice to every form and every gray, from hope to fullness—and then begins again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reimagines Velázquez’s *Las Meninas* in a deeply personal and imaginative way. Rather than simply describing the figures as they appear in the original painting, the speaker transforms them into creations of their own mind. The meninas become “their” meninas: figures reshaped by memory, emotion, and artistic vision. This personal reinterpretation allows the painting to move beyond its historical and visual context, becoming instead a living space where the speaker’s imagination takes control.

In this reimagining, the meninas are never fixed or stable. They are portrayed as constantly changing in mood, color, and meaning, much like the moon as it passes through different phases. At one moment, they may seem bright, playful, or full of life; at another, they may appear shadowed, melancholic, or mysterious. Their identities shift depending on the speaker’s perception, suggesting that art is not something with one permanent meaning, but something that changes with each act of looking.

The poem also emphasizes strong contrasts. Humor exists beside sadness, light beside darkness, and joy beside despair. These oppositions give the meninas emotional depth and complexity. They are not simple or decorative figures, nor are they reduced to a single feeling or role. Instead, they embody the contradictions of human experience. Their presence can be amusing and unsettling, beautiful and tragic, familiar and strange all at once.

Because of this, the figures are not presented as static puppets controlled by the painter or by tradition. They become complex theatrical presences, almost like actors on a stage. The speaker’s imagination gives them movement, voice, and emotional force. They seem to perform different roles, shifting their expressions and meanings as though participating in an ongoing drama. This theatrical quality makes them feel alive, even though they originate in a famous still image.

Ultimately, the speaker sees the meninas as endlessly shifting beings connected to art, memory, and perception. They belong to Velázquez’s painting, but they also belong to the speaker’s inner world. Their meaning emerges from the relationship between the artwork and the person who looks at it. In this way, the poem suggests that art is never entirely fixed in the past. It continues to change as it is remembered, imagined, and reinterpreted by each viewer.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the relationship between artistic reinterpretation and identity by invoking Picasso’s reimagining of Velázquez’s *Las Meninas*. Rather than treating the original painting as a fixed and untouchable masterpiece, the poem presents it as something alive—an image capable of being remade, recolored, rearranged, and personally claimed. Through references to Picasso, Velázquez, and “my meninas,” the speaker places themself within a long artistic conversation, suggesting that every act of looking is also an act of creation.

The poem’s imagery is marked by constant change. Colors shift, moods alter, light moves across the scene, and the figures seem to take on different roles, almost as if they are performers on a stage. This theatrical quality emphasizes the unstable nature of perception: what we see depends on angle, atmosphere, memory, and imagination. The meninas are not merely historical figures from a famous painting; they become projections of the speaker’s own vision, shaped by emotion and renewed each time they are encountered.

At the same time, the poem suggests that change does not erase permanence. Although “my meninas” are endlessly transformable, they also endure. Their identities are not destroyed by reinterpretation; instead, they are strengthened by it. Like Picasso’s variations on Velázquez, the poem shows that art survives because it can be seen differently across time. Its meaning is not confined to one version, one artist, or one moment.

Ultimately, the poem argues that the significance of art lies in continual transformation. A masterpiece remains powerful not because it stays the same, but because it invites new ways of seeing. Through personal vision, shifting imagery, and renewed perception, the speaker discovers that art is both inherited and remade. “My meninas” therefore become a symbol of artistic freedom: always changing, always returning, and always capable of revealing something new.
outputs.L5:
Pablo Picasso’s *Las Meninas* is one of the most fascinating reinterpretations in modern art. Inspired by Diego Velázquez’s famous 1656 painting *Las Meninas*, Picasso created a series of works in 1957 that transformed the original scene into his own bold, experimental style.

In Velázquez’s masterpiece, the young Infanta Margarita is surrounded by her attendants, known as “meninas,” while the painter himself appears in the background of the composition. Picasso admired this painting deeply, but instead of copying it, he reimagined it through Cubist forms, sharp lines, and dramatic contrasts. His version breaks the figures into geometric shapes and gives the scene a new emotional intensity.

Picasso’s *Las Meninas* series shows his dialogue with the past. He respected the old masters, but he also challenged tradition by turning a classical image into something modern and personal. Through these works, Picasso demonstrated that art is not only about imitation, but also about interpretation, transformation, and creativity.

Today, Picasso’s *Las Meninas* remains an important example of how one artist can respond to another across centuries, creating a bridge between Spanish Baroque painting and twentieth-century modern art.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem inspired by Picasso’s reinterpretations of Velázquez’s Las Meninas, beginning with the quote “I would try to do it in my way, forgetting Velázquez…”
counterfactuals.output:
“I would try to do it in my way, forgetting Velázquez…”

and the room fractures open—

not into memory,
but into angles,

into a palace of black lines
and staring lamps,
where the infanta becomes
a small sun
trapped in a grid of glances.

The dog is almost a shadow.
The maids are masks of light.
The painter stands everywhere at once,
his brush a knife,
his canvas a door
no one can stop opening.

Velázquez had made a mirror
and placed the world inside it.

Picasso takes the mirror
and breaks it carefully,
piece by piece,
until every shard
learns to look back.

Here is the princess,
not preserved,
but repeated—

blue, white, gray,
a child made of windows,
a face remembered
by someone who refuses
to remember plainly.

Here is the room again,
larger than Spain,
smaller than an eye.

Here is the king,
or only the idea of a king,
dissolving at the rear wall.

Here is the old master,
not forgotten,
but painted over
like a heartbeat
beneath another heartbeat.

And here is Picasso,
turning the scene
as one turns a question
in the hand:

What remains of a painting
when obedience leaves it?

What remains of a name
when another name
answers?

In the end,
the meninas do not stand still.

They multiply.
They shift.
They step out of their velvet weather

and enter the century
with square faces,
burning whites,
and the strange freedom
of being seen again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an ekphrastic poem about “my meninas” that blends references to Velázquez, Picasso, the moon, puppets, mirrors, the dog, the dwarf, and the man behind the easel.
counterfactuals.output:
**My Meninas**

In my room the meninas gather again,  
not in Madrid, not in oil, but in moonlight—  
silver spilled across the floorboards  
like milk from an overturned jug.

Velázquez stands behind the easel,  
or someone wearing his shadow does,  
his brush lifted like a question  
he has been asking for centuries.

In the mirror, the king and queen  
are small as coins,  
small as secrets,  
small as faces painted on the eyes of puppets.

Picasso arrives late,  
breaking the room into blue knives,  
black ladders, white masks—  
he makes the little maids angular,  
turns their gowns into folded paper storms,  
teaches the dog to sleep in cubes.

The dog does not care for history.  
He rests his heavy head  
on the threshold between court and dream,  
one paw in Spain,  
one paw in my childhood.

The dwarf looks straight through me.  
Not past me—through.  
As if I am the canvas,  
as if I am the royal ghost  
caught where the mirror should be.

Above us, the moon hangs  
like another pale infanta,  
round-faced, overdressed in clouds,  
watched by servants of light.  
It pulls invisible strings  
from every wrist and ribbon.

Then all the meninas move:  
a curtsy, a tilt, a painted blink.  
Their skirts rustle with wooden joints.  
Their mouths open and close  
on the same silent word.

Who is holding the strings?  
The man behind the easel?  
The mirror?  
Picasso with his fractured hands?  
The moon, that old puppeteer?

Or me—  
standing in front of the picture,  
wanting to enter,  
wanting to be seen,  
while my meninas, bright and unfinished,  
turn their faces toward me  
and begin to paint back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem in the style of a modern art meditation on Las Meninas, using shifting imagery of black and white, color, pathos, humor, and changeability.
counterfactuals.output:
**Afterimage with Infanta**

In the room, black gathers first—  
not as night, but as varnish,  
as the thinking part of light.

White arrives late,  
wearing a little dog’s boredom,  
the stiff cream of a dress  
too young to understand ceremony,  
too ceremonial to be childhood.

Between them: a painter  
standing inside his own question,  
brush lifted like a priest,  
or a waiter,  
or a man who has forgotten  
why he entered the kitchen.

Look closely:  
the canvas is a door,  
the door is a mirror,  
the mirror is a joke  
played by time on everybody  
with a face.

The king and queen float  
in the rear wall’s silver puddle—  
two postage stamps  
sent from authority  
to the address of the eye.

And the dwarf smiles sideways,  
because someone must know  
the empire has shoelaces,  
dust, indigestion,  
a spaniel dreaming of sausages  
beneath the tremendous architecture  
of being seen.

O black sleeve,  
O white cuff,  
O red ribbon burning  
like a small revolution  
on the child’s bodice—

color enters shyly, then all at once:  
rose in the cheek,  
gold in the hair,  
a greenish air  
where history has been breathing  
behind closed curtains.

Nothing stays where it is.

The girl becomes a chandelier,  
the dog becomes a cloud,  
the painter becomes a wall  
through which the future looks back  
and says: almost.

The maids lean inward,  
petals around a question.  
Their faces hold that tender exhaustion  
of people paid to witness splendor  
without touching it.

What is a portrait  
but a room learning to doubt itself?

What is power  
but a frame pretending  
it does not need the nail?

In the far doorway,  
a man pauses on the stair,  
half shadow, half exit,  
carrying the whole painting away  
one step at a time.

Stay, says the light.

Go, says the dark.

The child blinks.  
The brush hesitates.  
The dog does not care.

And we, ridiculous and solemn,  
stand where the monarchs stood,  
crowned for a moment  
by looking—

then dethroned  
by the next glance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical poem responding to Picasso’s Meninas series, focusing on how the figures keep changing across variations and palettes.
counterfactuals.output:
In Picasso’s rooms the Infanta will not stay still.  
She is a small bell struck in fifty-eight metals,  
a white flame, a yellow hinge, a black equation  
opening and closing where Velázquez left a door.  

Each canvas revises the weather of her body:  
now her skirt is a cubed cloud, now a paper lantern,  
now the dress fractures into milk, ash, arsenic green.  
Her face becomes a mask becoming a mirror  
becoming the sharp idea of a face.  

The maids lean in—then scatter—  
their courtesy broken into blue triangles,  
their hands like startled birds  
remembering and forgetting the ritual of service.  
The dwarf hardens to a carved question.  
The dog is a mound, a shadow, a golden sleep,  
then less than a dog: the gravity of being watched.  

Behind them all, the painter multiplies himself—  
a dark mast, a nail, a crossbeam of seeing—  
lifting his brush like a match  
to set the old palace burning in variations.  
Black-and-white: the room is an X-ray of power.  
Rose and ochre: blood warms the plaster.  
Acid colors arrive like rumors from another century,  
violet gnawing at lace, green biting the royal air.  

No one remains identical.  
Rank slips its costume. Light changes its mind.  
The princess is child, idol, pawn, aperture;  
the mirror at the back keeps swallowing the king and queen  
until they are only a pale hesitation,  
a sovereign blur in the throat of the room.  

To look is to unmake.  
To paint again is to confess  
the first world was never finished—  
only posed, powdered, waiting  
for the bull of the hand to enter  
and toss its gold furniture into stars.  

So the Meninas turn, dissolve, return:  
a court of fugitives trapped in pigment,  
each palette another fate,  
each line a knife teaching ceremony how to dance.  
Velázquez’s silence becomes Picasso’s weather,  
and every altered figure, burning through its borrowed name,  
keeps asking:  
who is real here,  
the watcher, the watched,  
or the change between them?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that opens with a Pablo Picasso quotation about painting his own Meninas, then explores “my meninas” through surreal images of moonlight, mirrors, puppetry, and despair.
counterfactuals.output:
“If someone wants to copy *Las Meninas*, entirely in good faith,  
I would try to do it in my own way, forgetting Velázquez.” —Pablo Picasso

My meninas arrive at moonrise,  
not girls, not ladies-in-waiting,  
but pale hinges of light  
opening and closing in the throat.

They carry mirrors under their arms  
like severed windows,  
each one reflecting a room  
where no one has ever been born.

The moon kneels in the basin,  
washing its face with milk and ashes;  
the floor tilts toward sleep,  
and the walls whisper in blue.

My meninas are puppets  
with strings tied to distant stars,  
their wooden hands raised gently  
to comfort the king of dust.

Behind them, a dog made of shadow  
dreams of being a door.  
Behind the dog, a painter  
paints himself disappearing.

Every mirror breeds another mirror,  
every candle invents a wound.  
The night pulls its black glove on  
and strokes the cheek of despair.

O my meninas, small moons in mourning,  
maids of the impossible room,  
who taught you to stand so still  
while the ceiling fills with rain?

One smiles with a porcelain crack.  
One weeps pearls into her sleeves.  
One holds a marionette of my heart  
and makes it bow, bow, bow.

In the corner, moonlight combs  
the hair of an empty chair.  
A crown floats upside down  
in a glass of bitter water.

I call them mine  
because they will not leave me—  
these silver children of the mirror,  
these attendants of the dark.

They gather around my bed at dawn,  
their faces unfinished,  
and ask me to paint them again  
with a brush made of despair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
